title: Gardening for Beginners: How to Start Your First Garden
hook: Starting a garden sounds easy, until the plants die and you don't know why. The good news is that a small, well-planned first garden almost always works. Here are seven steps to grow your first plants, with no experience needed, and what to do when plants struggle.
intro: Most beginners fail for three reasons. They plant in the wrong spot, they start far too big, and they pick plants that are difficult to grow. We'll avoid all three. You'll choose a sunny place, build a small bed, improve the soil, and grow easy plants that reward you quickly. A garden the size of a doormat can feed you salad for weeks, so don't worry about space. We'll go step by step, and by the end you will have a clear plan, ready to put into the ground this weekend.
youNeedNarration: Here's what you need. A sunny spot, outdoors or on a balcony. Some compost and garden soil. A trowel and a pair of gloves. A few seed packets or small plants from a garden center. And a watering can or a hose with a gentle spray head. Nothing here is expensive, and many people already own most of it. If you plan to use pots, add a few containers with drainage holes.
heroImagePrompt: A small neat raised garden bed with young lettuce and herbs, watering can beside it, morning sunlight, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Pick a sunny spot
steps.narration: Step one. Watch your yard or balcony during the day, and find the place that gets at least six to eight hours of direct sun. Most vegetables and flowers need that much light to grow strongly. Also look for easy access to water, because a garden far from a tap will soon be neglected. Avoid low spots where water collects after rain, and places right beside large trees, whose roots steal moisture. If you have very little sun, don't give up. Leafy greens and herbs like mint and parsley do well with about four hours. Take a few minutes to note it down, because the whole garden depends on this single choice.
steps.tip: Six to eight hours of sun
steps.mistake: Planting in a shady or soggy corner
steps.imagePrompt: A sunny patch of lawn in a backyard with long shadows and a wooden fence, early morning light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Start small
steps.narration: Step two. Resist the urge to dig up half the yard. A first garden should be about four feet by four feet, or roughly one metre by one metre, or a few pots. That size is small enough to water and weed in ten minutes a day, but big enough to grow real food. You can build a simple raised bed from wooden boards, or just mark out a square in the lawn. Next year, if it goes well, you can always make it bigger. A small success is a better start than a big failure. You will learn much faster from a tiny bed that you look after every day.
steps.mistake: Digging a huge bed you can't maintain
steps.imagePrompt: An empty small wooden raised garden bed on grass, freshly built, garden tools beside it, bright daylight, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Prepare the soil
steps.narration: Step three. Good soil matters more than almost anything else. Remove grass and weeds from your square, then loosen the top ten inches or twenty-five centimetres with a fork or spade. Mix in a few inches of compost, which adds nutrients and helps the soil hold water while still draining. Squeeze a handful of soil. If it forms a ball that crumbles when poked, it's just right. If it stays sticky, add more compost, and if it falls apart as dust, add more compost as well. Do this a week before planting if you can, so the bed has time to settle.
steps.imagePrompt: Gloved hands mixing dark compost into garden soil with a trowel in a raised bed, close-up, soft daylight, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Choose easy plants
steps.narration: Step four. Pick plants that forgive mistakes. Lettuce, radishes, green beans, zucchini, cherry tomatoes and herbs like basil are all great for beginners. Radishes can be ready in about a month, which is a wonderful confidence boost. Marigolds add color and attract helpful insects. Choose plants that you like to eat, and check the seed packet or plant label, which tells you the best planting season for your area. Buy small plants if you want faster results, and seeds if you want to save money. Don't plant too many of one thing at once, because ten lettuces ripen together. Plant a few every two weeks instead.
steps.tip: Radishes are ready in about a month
steps.mistake: Planting things you will never eat
steps.imagePrompt: A wooden table with colorful vegetable seed packets, small seedlings in pots and a trowel, natural light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Plant at the right depth
steps.narration: Step five. Follow the instructions on the seed packet for spacing and depth. As a rule, small seeds are planted shallowly, about twice their own thickness, while seedlings go in at the same depth they sat in their pot. Gently loosen the roots, set the plant in a hole, firm the soil around it and water right away. Space plants as the label says, even if it looks too wide, because crowded plants get disease and produce less. Add a label so you remember what is growing where. A wooden stick and a pencil are enough. Gently press the soil down and avoid stepping on the bed.
steps.tip: Give them the spacing on the label
steps.imagePrompt: A hand planting a small green seedling into dark garden soil with a trowel, rows of young plants behind, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Water the right way
steps.narration: Step six. Most gardens need about one inch of water per week, from rain and watering combined. Water deeply but less often, so roots grow downward in search of moisture. It's better to give the bed a slow, thorough soak twice a week than a quick sprinkle every day. Water in the morning, aim at the base of the plants and not the leaves, and use a gentle spray. To check, push a finger two inches into the soil. If it's dry there, it's time to water. In hot weather, containers dry out much faster than garden beds, so check them every day. Mulch also helps a great deal here.
steps.imagePrompt: A metal watering can pouring water gently at the base of young vegetable plants, morning light, droplets, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Mulch, weed and check weekly
steps.narration: Step seven. Spread a layer of mulch, such as straw, shredded leaves or bark, about two inches thick around your plants. It keeps the soil moist, slows weeds, and protects roots from heat. Then make a habit of walking through your garden once or twice a week. Pull any small weeds, look under leaves for pests, and pick vegetables when they are ripe, because regular picking encourages more. Ten minutes of attention each week does more than one big session each month. Seeing your plants grow is the best motivation, so take a photo every week.
steps.tip: Ten minutes a week beats one big job
steps.imagePrompt: Golden straw mulch spread around healthy green vegetable plants in a small garden bed, soft sunlight, photorealistic, no text

bonus.label: NOT WORKING?
bonus.title: If your plants struggle
bonus.narration: Every beginner meets problems, and most are easy to read. Yellow leaves and soggy soil usually mean too much water, so let the soil dry. Holes in leaves point to slugs or caterpillars, which you can pick off by hand in the evening. Tall, weak seedlings need more light. Change one thing at a time, so you learn what worked.
bonus.tip: Change only one thing at a time
bonus.imagePrompt: A close-up of a green garden plant with a few yellowing leaves in dark soil, a gardener's hand gently holding one leaf. Photorealistic photograph for a how-to video. Bright natural light, clean and uncluttered. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

bonus.label: GO FURTHER
bonus.title: Grow more next year
bonus.narration: Once your first bed works, you can grow more. Sow a second round of radishes or lettuce every two weeks, so harvests keep coming. Add a second bed or a few extra pots, and start a small compost bin for free fertilizer. Write down what you planted and when, because those notes will be worth more than any book.
bonus.imagePrompt: A wicker basket of fresh radishes, lettuce and herbs on a wooden garden bench, a small raised bed in the background. Photorealistic photograph for a how-to video. Bright natural light, clean and uncluttered. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

bonus.label: PREVENTION
bonus.title: Prevent common problems
bonus.narration: A few habits stop most problems early. Water at the base of the plants, early in the day, so leaves can dry. Do not grow the same crop in the same spot every year, because pests build up in the soil. Pick off sick leaves quickly, and choose plants that suit your climate.
bonus.imagePrompt: A watering can pouring a gentle stream at the base of young vegetable plants in a small garden bed, morning sunlight. Photorealistic photograph for a how-to video. Bright natural light, clean and uncluttered. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

mistakesToAvoid.narration: Let's finish with the mistakes that stop most new gardeners. One, planting too much, too soon, which leads to overwhelm and a neglected plot. Two, overwatering. More plants die from too much water than too little, especially in pots with no drainage holes. And three, ignoring your local planting calendar. Planting tomatoes before the last frost, or lettuce in midsummer heat, is a recipe for disappointment. Start small, check your soil, and be patient. Every gardener has lost a few plants, and each mistake is a lesson.
items: Starting with a garden that is too big

recap.narration: Let's recap. Pick a sunny spot. Start small. Prepare the soil with compost. Choose easy plants. Plant at the right depth and spacing. Water deeply and less often. And mulch, weed and check your garden every week. Follow these seven steps, and you'll be picking your own food in a matter of weeks. The bonus sections cover problems, next year and prevention.

outro: That's how you start your first garden. If you're growing something this year, subscribe to WikiTube, because we publish a new how-to every single day. Tell us in the comments what you plan to grow first, and what you would like us to explain next. See you tomorrow.

metadata.title: Gardening for Beginners: How to Start Your First Garden
metadata.description:
Want to grow your own food or flowers but have no idea where to start? In this step-by-step video on gardening for beginners, you'll learn how to start your first garden: pick a sunny spot, start small, prepare the soil with compost, choose easy plants, plant at the right depth, water properly, and mulch. A simple plan that works in a yard, on a balcony or in pots.

You'll need: a sunny spot outdoors, compost and garden soil, a trowel and gloves, seeds or small plants, a watering can or hose.
